paragraphs: As soon as the arrangements were complete for our voyage to Italy, Paul and several other prisoners were put under the charge of a centurion named Julius, from an elite regiment. We boarded a ship from Adramyttium that was headed for ports along the Asia coast and westward. Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica, came with us.
The next day we docked at Sidon. Julius treated Paul kindly — he let him go ashore and enjoy the hospitality of his friends there.

Back out at sea, we sailed north along the sheltered side of Cyprus, northeast of the island, because strong westerly winds were against us, then westward along the coast to the port of Myra. There the centurion found an Egyptian grain ship bound for Italy and transferred us aboard. We hit rough weather and couldn't hold our course. After a long, hard struggle, we finally reached the southern coast of Crete and docked at Fair Havens — fitting name!

By now we'd lost a lot of time. The autumn sailing season was over, so from here through winter it would be stormy — too dangerous for sailing. Paul warned them: "I can see nothing but disaster ahead for the cargo and the ship — not to mention our lives — if we set sail now." But Fair Havens wasn't a great harbor for spending the winter. Phoenix, a few miles farther along, was much better. The centurion ignored Paul's warning and let the ship's captain and owner talk him into trying for the next harbor.

When a gentle south wind started blowing, they weighed anchor, thinking it would be smooth sailing. But no sooner were they out at sea than a hurricane-force wind — the infamous northeaster — slammed into them. They lost all control of the ship. It was like a cork in the storm.

We ran under the shelter of a small island called Cauda and barely managed to secure the lifeboat and take in sail. Rocky shoals kept us from getting close to shore. We only avoided them by dropping sea anchors.

The next day, back out on the open sea and badly battered by the storm, we threw the cargo overboard. On the third day the crew lightened the ship further by tossing all the tackle and gear. For days we hadn't seen sun or stars. Wind and waves were pounding us mercilessly, and we lost all hope of being rescued.

With everyone's appetite for food — and for life — long gone, Paul stood up among us and said, "Friends, you really should have listened to me back in Crete. We could have avoided all this damage and loss. But no point dwelling on that now. From here on, things are looking up! I can promise you that not one of us will drown — though I can't say the same for the ship. The ship is doomed."

"Last night an angel of God stood beside me — the God I serve — and said, 'Don't be afraid, Paul. You still have to stand trial before Caesar — and God has graciously given you the lives of everyone sailing with you.' So take heart, friends! I believe God will do exactly what he told me. But we are going to run aground on some island."

On the fourteenth night, drifting somewhere in the Adriatic Sea, around midnight the sailors sensed land was near. They dropped a weighted line and measured about 120 feet deep; a little later, about 90 feet. Afraid we'd run aground on the rocks, they dropped four anchors from the stern and prayed for daylight.

Some of the sailors tried to abandon ship. They lowered the lifeboat, pretending they were going to drop more anchors from the bow. Paul saw right through it and told the centurion and the soldiers, "Unless these sailors stay with the ship, we're all going down." So the soldiers cut the lifeboat's ropes and let it drift away.

Just before dawn, Paul gathered everyone and suggested breakfast: "Today is the fourteenth day you've gone without food. None of you has felt like eating! But I'm urging you to eat something now. You'll need your strength for what's ahead. You're going to come through this without a scratch!"
He broke bread, thanked God, passed it around, and they all ate heartily — 276 of us in all! With the meal over and everyone full, they lightened the ship further by dumping the grain into the sea.

At daybreak, no one recognized the land — but then they spotted a bay with a sandy beach. They decided to try running the ship aground there. They cut the anchor ropes, untied the rudders, hoisted the foresail, and headed for the beach with the wind behind them. But they didn't make it. Still far from shore, they struck a sandbar, and the ship started breaking apart.

The soldiers decided to kill the prisoners so none could swim away and escape — but the centurion, determined to save Paul, stopped them. He ordered everyone who could swim to jump overboard first and head for shore, and the rest to grab planks or pieces of the ship. Everyone made it to land safely.
title: The Great Storm and the Shipwreck
